Silver fell 2.89% this morning — nearly four times gold's move — and this paper's platinum and palladium hold just ended.

Kitco read gold at $4,360.00, silver $63.12, platinum $1,726.00 and palladium $1,274.00 at 05:58 New York, confirmed on a second page. Every mark is lower than yesterday's: gold down $33.10 (0.75%), silver down $1.88 (2.89%), platinum down $23.00 (1.32%), palladium down $37.00 (2.82%).

Platinum and palladium had carried stale 17 August marks for three sessions because their two source pages wouldn't agree. This morning both held marks sat above every live price on the table — a mark above the whole range isn't a mark — so the hold ended and both were written at Kitco's reading.

The driver, per both outside sources: bond yields. The 30-year Treasury hit 5.31%, its highest since June 2007.

The lab-grown wholesale index is down 96% since 2018. The retail markup over wholesale hasn't moved more than a point or two in years.

JCK's 10 August figures, drawn from Edahn Golan's Q2 wholesale list: the index fell 13% in the year to Q2 2026 after a 26% drop in 2025, yet retail markups still run above 80% over wholesale. Inside the series the decline isn't uniform — one-carat rounds rose 1% year on year, while two-carat stones fell 20%.

The number worth watching: US lab-grown inventory-to-sales at retail has climbed from single digits in 2020 to nearly 50%. That's what turns a falling wholesale price into a write-down instead of a margin.

This paper's own tape reads $704 for a one-carat lab-grown reference. A six-retailer sample from 25 July found $550 for the same stone — a 28.0% gap.

Rolex made Drake a one-off. Nobody, including Rolex, has published a price for it. The one number anyone can stand behind belongs to a different watch.

A gem-set Daytona described as a piece unique reached Drake on 16 August — no reference number, no stone count, no carat weight, no price, and no statement from Rolex. Trade press has called it precedent-breaking; this desk found no documentation for that claim, and the same reporting names a prior claimed one-off from 2024.

The only transacted figure: a Rolex GMT-Master II Drake once owned sold this year through dealer Wind Vintage for $500,000 — the full advertised ask, roughly five times average dealer value, after four offers. That watch had a reference, a provenance and a price. The new one has none of the three.
